settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: getJavaAlgorithm (lines 20-33) only maps HS256/HS384/HS512 and throws IllegalArgumentException for anything else, so a non-HMAC alg in the header fails rather than silently downgrading.
The MAC is computed over input.getContent(), i.e., the actual signed header+payload, so a changed header changes the signed content.
Comparison is a String.equals on Base64 URL-encoded values, which is standard in this codebase; no explicit remote-attacker timing oracle is demonstrated within the read spans.
candidates.description: In HMACProvider.verify(JWSInput,SecretKey) (lines 79-91) and verify(JWSInput,byte[]) (lines 95-107), the expected signature is recomputed by calling sign(input.getContent(), input.getHeader().getAlgorithm(), key) and then Base64-url-encoded and compared against the signature carried in the token (input.getEncodedSignature()) using String.equals (lines 84-85 and 100-101). Two concerns follow: (1) the comparison is not constant-time, so an attacker able to measure response timing could in principle recover the expected MAC byte-by-byte; (2) the MAC algorithm is selected from the token header (line 83/99), so the library relies entirely on the caller to pin the expected algorithm/key and does not itself reject algorithm substitution. The header algorithm is also used to pick the Java algorithm in getJavaAlgorithm (lines 20-33), which throws for non-HMAC algorithms. This is a library-side design/API hardening gap; whether it is exploitable depends on how callers use it, which is outside the read spans.
missing_evidence: Call sites of HMACProvider.verify to determine whether the algorithm is pinned by the caller and whether the value is derived from untrusted network input.
Evidence that timing differences are remotely measurable (network noise, JIT) and a concrete attack path.
Whether constant-time comparison utilities are available/used elsewhere in the project.
preconditions: Application code calls HMACProvider.verify with an attacker-influenced JWSInput and a secret key.
Attacker is able to issue many verification requests and observe timing differences.
Caller does not independently pin/verify the header algorithm before verification.
candidates.title: HMACProvider.verify compares recomputed and supplied JWS signature with non-constant-time String.equals and trusts header algorithm

counter_evidence: writeTo is the writer path; the Source object is normally produced by application code rather than taken directly from the request body, so attacker control is not established within the read spans.

readFrom (lines 45-50) simply returns a StreamSource over the entity stream and performs no parsing there; parsing only happens if/when this StreamSource is later transformed on a write, which is typical output, not input.
No evidence within the read spans that any resource forwards attacker-controlled XML into a returned Source.
candidates.description: SourceProvider.writeTo (lines 62-100) takes a caller-supplied Source. When it is a StreamSource it wraps the underlying InputStream/Reader into an InputSource and then creates the SAX reader used for the transform with SAXParserFactory.newInstance().newSAXParser().getXMLReader() (line 81), and performs the transform with TransformerFactory.newInstance().newTransformer() (line 85). Neither factory is configured with disallow-doctype-decl, external-general/parameter-entities=false, or accessExternalDTD restrictions, in contrast with the hardening used elsewhere in the project (e.g., DocumentProvider.readFrom lines 118-121). If the Source content is attacker-influenced, the XML processing performed during the transform could resolve external entities (XXE/SSRF/local file disclosure). No such configuration is applied on this path.
missing_evidence: A concrete resource/provider that pipes request XML into a Source which is then written through SourceProvider.writeTo.
The default JDK parser behavior in the deployment (whether disallow-doctype-decl defaults on) to confirm concrete XXE impact.
Tests or call sites demonstrating attacker control of the transformed Source content.
preconditions: A JAX-RS resource method returns a Source (StreamSource) whose content is derived from untrusted input.
The Source is serialized via SourceProvider.writeTo, causing the SAX parse/transform to run over attacker-controlled XML.
candidates.title: SourceProvider.writeTo builds a SAX reader/Transformer without XXE hardening for caller-supplied StreamSource

counter_evidence: Defaults are secure: expandEntityReferences=false, enableSecureProcessingFeature=true, disableDTDs=true (lines 45-47), so out-of-the-box behavior blocks doctype/external entities.
Config is read only once in the constructor from ResteasyConfiguration; the values are operator/deployment settings, not request parameters.
No code path within the read spans shows request-controlled input reaching these configuration values.
candidates.description: DocumentProvider holds three security-relevant flags whose defaults are safe (expandEntityReferences=false, enableSecureProcessingFeature=true, disableDTDs=true at lines 45-47), but all three are read from ResteasyConfiguration in the constructor (lines 76-100). In readFrom (lines 109-140) these flags are applied to the DocumentBuilderFactory: setExpandEntityReferences(expandEntityReferences), FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING=enableSecureProcessingFeature, disallow-doctype-decl=disableDTDs, and external-general-entities/external-parameter-entities=expandEntityReferences (lines 118-122). When expandEntityReferences is turned on, the code explicitly sets accessExternalDTD to "all" (lines 123-133). Consequently, if RESTEASY_EXPAND_ENTITY_REFERENCES / RESTEASY_SECURE_PROCESSING_FEATURE / RESTEASY_DISABLE_DTDS are set to weakening values (via configuration an operator or, in some deployments, an attacker-influenced source may control), the parser would allow DTDs/external entities and enable XXE during readFrom of untrusted request bodies. The shared, lazily-initialized DocumentBuilderFactory instance (lines 56-68) also means the feature flags are re-applied on each readFrom.
missing_evidence: Evidence that RESTEASY_EXPAND_ENTITY_REFERENCES/RESTEASY_DISABLE_DTDS/RESTEASY_SECURE_PROCESSING_FEATURE can be influenced by an unauthenticated actor in a realistic deployment.
The precedence/defaults applied by ResteasyConfiguration when the parameters are absent, to confirm they cannot be nulled in a way that disables checks.
preconditions: Deployment configuration sets resteasy.document.expand.entity.references=true and/or resteasy.document.disable.dtds=false and/or secure processing off.
An attacker can submit XML request bodies to an endpoint that consumes Document.
candidates.title: DocumentProvider XXE hardening is fully configurable and can be weakened via ResteasyConfiguration parameters

counter_evidence: getJavaAlgorithm only accepts RS256/RS384/RS512 and throws IllegalArgumentException for other algorithms (lines 20-28), preventing alg=none or HMAC confusion via this path.
Signature verification uses java.security.Signature.verify (line 66), not a manual/equality comparison, so no signature-bypass comparison flaw is present here.
No caller code within the read spans is shown to skip algorithm validation.
candidates.description: RSAProvider.verify(JWSInput,PublicKey) (lines 59-72) computes the verifier by calling getSignature(input.getHeader().getAlgorithm()) (line 63), i.e., the algorithm identifier from the token header, and only maps RS256/RS384/RS512 inside getJavaAlgorithm (lines 17-30). The signature comparison itself is delegated to java.security.Signature.verify(input.getSignature()) (line 66), which is correct and non-string-comparison based. The residual concern is algorithm-agility handling: the library does not pin the expected algorithm and relies on the caller, so a caller that does not validate alg against an allow-list could be induced to use a different RSA variant. Because only RS* values are accepted (others throw IllegalArgumentException, lines 27-28), classic HMAC/none algorithm-confusion is not reachable through this method alone.
missing_evidence: Call sites of RSAProvider.verify to confirm whether the caller enforces an algorithm allow-list.
Whether any related verification entry point (not in the read spans) performs key/algorithm consistency checks.
preconditions: Application code calls RSAProvider.verify with a token whose header algorithm is attacker-controlled and does not independently constrain the accepted algorithm.
candidates.title: RSAProvider.verify selects signature algorithm from untrusted JWS header without internal pinning
